title: Transient slab occupancy and request-backlog investigation
content:
Objective:
This note captures an investigation into a pattern of intermittent OOMs seen on multi-tenant pools during 99th-percentile latency spikes. The behavior looks different from long-running leakage or static fragmentation: short-lived slab occupancy spikes appear correlated with small bursts of concurrent requests causing cudaMalloc backpressure and allocator slowdown. Goal is to document observations, reproduce steps, test hypotheses, and propose mitigations.

Summary of symptom:
- Instances: g4dn-like GPU pools running runtime v2.4.x.
- Symptom: transient OOMs (process-level) lasting 1–10s, then automatic recovery.
- Triggers: sudden small bursts of concurrent requests (5–20 reqs) each requesting long sequence lengths (>2k tokens) or cache-miss prompts.
- Not consistent with cumulative leak: total resident memory returns to baseline after spike.
- Logs show many failed cudaMalloc attempts with retries and then a cascade of allocator retries causing latency and eventual OOM on one task.

Repro steps used locally:
1) Start a local replica of the pool with two models loaded (opt-6.7b and opt-13b-quant).
2) Use the synthetic load script (tools/bench/synthetic-burst.py) to send 15 concurrent requests with seq_len=2300 and no K/V cache hot-keys.
3) Observe runtime logs and /proc/meminfo + nvidia-smi while increasing concurrency.
4) Capture allocator debug log (ENV: REDWOOD_ALLOC_TRACE=1) and coredump on OOM if triggered.

Observed telemetry (representative run 2024-11-06):
- Baseline resident set: 12.4 GB.
- During burst: resident peaked at 14.9 GB for ~3s then back to 12.5 GB.
- Kernel-level cudaMalloc failure/retry window: ~750ms total across many retries.
- Allocator free-list fragmentation metric: small-slot pools show transient occupancy spikes from 60% -> 92% used.
- Number of outstanding allocation ops during spike: ~120
- Average per-allocation latency during spike: 6.8ms (vs 0.4ms baseline).
- RPC latency P99 increased from 120ms -> 3.2s correlated with allocation retries.

Important logs (abridged):
- "cudaMalloc failed: out of memory, retrying (attempt 3/5)" repeated across worker threads.
- "eviction: cannot free contiguous slab of 8MB, scanning small-slab list"
- "alloc_trace: slab_alloc: allocated Chunk@0x7f9c... size=8MB from arena 3, free_list shrank"

Hypotheses:
H1: Burst concurrency creates many overlapping workspace allocations of mid-size blocks (2–16MB). These cause the allocator to temporarily deplete local small-slab caches, triggering slow path global coalescence and cudaMalloc calls which are serialized and backpressured by the CUDA driver.
H2: Some arena(s) become hot with fragmentation tombstones preventing coalescence fast enough; repeated small frees followed by new midsize allocs prevent reuse and force more cudaMallocs.
H3: KV cache policy (no shared prefix hits) forces allocation of transient KV snapshots, inflating working set and causing short-lived OOMs.

Experiments run and outcomes:
E1: Pre-warm mid-size slab pool before bursts.
- Method: allocate floor(peak_expected_mid_slots) at init time and hold them in a background pool.
- Result: transient OOMs eliminated in 12/15 reproduction runs; RPC P99 still increased but less (peak 900ms).
- Interpretation: reducing first-time cudaMallocs mitigates the slow-path latency.

E2: Reduce per-request workspace by applying conservative decoding buffer heuristics (limit pre-allocation to 75% of worst-case).
- Result: fewer mid-size allocs created; memory peak reduced by ~1.1GB. OOMs avoided in 10/15 runs.

E3: Force slab defragmentation between requests (synchronous coalesce).
- Method: after request completes, run a quick defrag pass that coalesces contiguous tombstones into larger free-chunks.
- Result: latency overhead high (avg +120ms), reduced fragmentation but increased CPU time and reduced throughput. Not acceptable in mainline.

E4: Try driver-level retry tuning (increase cudaMallocAsync thresholds) and enable cudamallocasync reservation bucket of 64MB blocks.
- Result: marginal improvement; still saw contention when many threads requested many different sizes.

Telemetry correlates:
- Slab occupancy spikes are tightly aligned with number of concurrent requests that cause cache-miss workspaces and with periods of reduced KV cache hit rate.
- Garbage collection/eviction window is typically 200–800ms after burst; during this time, free lists are in flux and many allocs hit slow paths.

Root cause (working summary):
The immediate cause is a synchronized rush of mid-size workspace allocations across threads that exhausts the allocator's hot free lists and forces many serialized device allocations (cudaMalloc or slow path in device memory manager). The allocator's coalescence heuristics are not aggressive enough under bursty concurrency, and tombstone fragmentation plus a lack of pre-warmed mid-size slabs make the process vulnerable to transient OOMs. The underlying CUDA driver behavior (cudaMalloc async serialization/backpressure) amplifies the latency and leads to cascading failures for some request handlers.

Short-term mitigations (low-risk):
- Pre-warm a mid-size slab pool on instance start (configurable via REDWOOD_PREWARM_SLAB_MB).
- Conservative workspace pre-allocation thresholds (limit worst-case > 75% to avoid huge transient allocations).
- Increase logging to capture allocation trace windows for suspected hosts (REDWOOD_ALLOC_DUMP_WINDOW=2000ms).

Medium-term changes (engineering work):
- Implement lightweight, lock-free per-core mid-size slab caches that can service 2–16MB allocations without global locks.
- Improve tombstone coalescence heuristics to detect when neighboring slots are free and lazily merge during peak idle points.
- Introduce a burst-mode allocator that trades a small memory headroom (configurable) to handle transient concurrency surges without going to cudaMalloc.

A/B tradeoffs considered:
- Synchronous defrag (works but high latency) vs background coalesce (more complex correctness).
- Larger static reservation improves resilience but increases steady-state memory and cost.

Action items / TODOs:
- [Priya] Add a prewarm flag and run a 72h soak on staging pool with synthetic bursts (due: 2025-02-28).
- [Daniel] Prototype per-core mid-size caches (spike) and microbench (due: 2025-03-14).
- [Marta] Add allocator trace instrumentation to tracing pipeline and dashboard (linked to JIRA-INF-2345).
- Create a short customer-facing one-pager for support explaining transient OOM root cause and recommended config (owner: Noah).

Notes for oncall / SRE:
- Short diagnostic checklist for incidents: collect allocator trace, nvidia-smi snapshots, process resident memory before/during/after, runtime logs with REDWOOD_ALLOC_TRACE.
- Recommended quick remediate: enable prewarm flag on the afflicted pool (hotfix) and scale up pool temporarily to absorb bursts.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- synthetic-burst runner: python tools/bench/synthetic-burst.py --concurrency 15 --seq-len 2300 --duration 60
- enable tracing: export REDWOOD_ALLOC_TRACE=1; export REDWOOD_ALLOC_DUMP_WINDOW=2000
- quick heap snapshot via gdb: run target process; p malloc_stats(); Note: guarded to avoid altering timings during production run.

References and related tickets:
- JIRA-INF-2345 (investigation placeholder)
- PR #789 implements prewarm option and basic metrics (https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/789)
- Slack thread: #allocator-debug (https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C01234567/p169)

Closing comment:
This investigation indicates the immediate path to reduce incident rate is pragmatic pre-warm and modest workspace limits. Long-term allocator improvements will give better throughput and avoid steady-state memory inflation. Will iterate on microbench data and reconvene after the staging soak to decide which medium-term changes to prioritize.
